title: free classes and guru dakshina
hookLine: should wisdom have a price? a rented room, and no tickets
carry: teaching is a gift; dakshina is the thanks
tomorrow: a week of guests and hosts. which line goes home with you?

lines: A PAYWALL BEFORE THE BEST PART.
cards: A good teacher can charge by the minute now: a course, a subscription, a paywall right before the best part. So here's the question: should wisdom have a price? Vivekananda answered with a room in New York.
Rented, plain, and crowded. Not enough chairs, so people sat on the floor. No ticket at the door.

teach.h: FREE CLASSES IN A RENTED ROOM.
teach.b: His disciples' biography describes it simply. In New York he rented rooms and taught classes free of charge: Vedanta, the teaching of the Upanishads, taught as practice, how to sit, how to breathe, how to watch the mind.
Out of those classes grew his book Raja Yoga, and his New York work gave the Vedanta Society of New York its start. Why free?
Because in Hindu tradition, sacred teaching isn't sold. The old law book of Manu frowns on teaching the Veda for a set fee.
Instead the student gives guru dakshina: a thank-you gift to the teacher, offered at the end, from the heart. The Bhagavata tells the most well-known one.
Krishna and his brother Balarama finish their studies with the sage Sandipani and ask what they can give. The teacher asks for the one thing money can't buy: his son, lost to the sea.

Krishna goes all the way to Yama, lord of death, and brings the boy home. That's dakshina: not a price, but a thank-you as big as love can make it. A neighbor tradition says something close, in its own words.
In the Gospel of Matthew, Jesus sends out his disciples to heal and to preach, and tells them: "freely ye have received, freely give." Shared: what was received as a gift goes out as a gift.
An honest difference: in Matthew, the disciples go out on the road and the homes that take them in feed them; in Hindu dakshina, the grateful student brings the gift back to the teacher.

how: Vedanta societies that grew from his work hold classes, readings and meditation; his book Raja-Yoga came out of the New York classes.

games.q: your uncle runs a free weekend Gita class at the temple. a grateful parent insists on paying. what fits the tradition?
o: charge everyone, so the tutoring is taken seriously.
close the class. free things get taken for granted.
keep it free, and welcome a thank-you gift, like dakshina.
games.why: sacred teaching isn't sold. the student, or the family, gives dakshina: a thank-you from the heart, not a fee.

practice: If there's paper near you, write down the name of one person who taught you something and never asked anything back. If there isn't, trace the name with a finger on your palm.
Then choose a small dakshina for them this week: a note, a call, a dish. Let the gift go back as a gift.
